rationale: A wins because it finds four usable press lanes and makes each one earn its keep with proof, caveats, and a real beat. Its “A meditation app now has more people covered than it has paying customers — six times over” is an actual business-model angle, not announcement confetti. B has bones, but “The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving” tries to turn one Calm deal into a market verdict before the evidence can carry it.
gaps_in_A: “at a moment when demand for care exceeds clinician supply” imports a public-health backdrop the update did not supply. A even refuses a similar crisis peg later, so this is the draft stepping on its own rake.
“on the plan's dime” implies payer economics even though the update says “no revenue terms disclosed.” The angle later asks the right question, but the headline already spent the money.
“reimbursement category” may be one notch too strong unless the coverage mechanism is confirmed. Covered benefit is in the facts; reimbursement is still a proof point.
gaps_in_B: “Health Insurers Start Covering Meditation Apps. The Wellness-to-Clinical Shift Is Arriving.” Plural apps and sweeping shift language from one Calm deal. That is how a trend piece gets laughed out of an editor meeting.
“Coverage Was the Last Wall” invents the barrier. The update gives covered lives, not evidence that insurance coverage was the final obstacle to access or usage.

“from pharmaceutical research, food science, and now digital health — is that funder effect persists” imports a whole outside argument not present in the update. Useful background after reporting; sloppy as generated grounding.

“Business/revenue mechanics — no_journalist_shape” throws away the best missing angle: 25 million covered members versus 4 million paid subscribers. No revenue terms is a proof gap, not a reason to kill the business-model story.
